title: The Harappan Civilisation

cards.b: The Indus or Harappan civilisation is the oldest urban culture of the subcontinent. It is asked every year: sites, planning, trade, decline and the script.

Dayaram Sahni found Harappa (1921); R. D. Banerji, Mohenjo-daro (1922); John Marshall was director general of the ASI. Mature phase: 2600 to 1900 BCE. Spread: Punjab, Sindh, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, western UP, Afghanistan (Shortugai). Sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi (largest in India), Chanhudaro, Surkotada, Ropar. Named “Indus Valley”, but many sites lay on the Ghaggar-Hakra.

Grid pattern; streets crossing at right angles; two parts: citadel (west) and lower town (east); baked brick in the ratio 1:2:4; covered drains with soak pits; the Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro); granaries (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro); Dholavira’s three parts and water reservoirs (UNESCO 2021); Lothal’s dockyard. Houses with courtyards, bathrooms and wells.

Wheat, barley, cotton, dates, peas; cattle (humped bull), sheep, goat. No clear evidence of the plough in most sites (a furrowed field at Kalibangan). Crafts: beads (Chanhudaro), pottery, bronze and copper work, seals of steatite. Trade: Mesopotamia (Meluhha in Sumerian texts); Persian Gulf, Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan; weights in multiples of 16; a lack of coins (barter). Raw materials: lapis lazuli (Shortugai), copper (Khetri), tin, shell.

Seals show the Pashupati figure, unicorn bull, and trees. Mother goddess terracotta; Lingam and yoni stones; tree and animal worship; fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal. Bronze Dancing Girl, steatite Priest-King. Burial: extended burials, pot burials. Society: no clear palaces or temples, suggesting a different form of authority.

About 400 signs on seals, mostly short; written right to left (boustrophedon in some). Not yet deciphered despite many attempts (Asko Parpola: Dravidian; S. R. Rao and others: Sanskrit-like; Iravatham Mahadevan: Dravidian). Without a bilingual text, decipherment is stalled. The Dholavira signboard of ten large signs is a famous find.

Theories: shift of the Saraswati-Ghaggar river and drought (4.2 ka event); flooding (Mohenjo-daro); Aryan invasion (Wheeler, now widely rejected); trade collapse; ecological stress. The mature phase ended about 1900 BCE; urban features faded, with late Harappan villages in the east. Most scholars favour gradual climate-linked decline and migration over invasion.

Wheeler (1947) read Rig Veda’s purandara as conquest of Harappan cities. Later, no evidence of mass violence was found at Mohenjo-daro. Ancient DNA work points two ways: the Rakhigarhi genome (Shinde et al., 2019) has no steppe ancestry, while Narasimhan et al. (2019) show steppe pastoralist ancestry entering South Asia around 2000 to 1500 BCE. The debate on origins is both scientific and political. Make a balanced answer.

Dholavira (Gujarat) became a World Heritage Site in 2021; Lothal’s National Maritime Heritage Complex is under construction. Rakhigarhi is being developed as a museum. The Harappan drains and water management are cited in modern town planning; Kutch and Rajasthan water storage echo it. Pakistan holds Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (UNESCO since 1980).
